Absolute trash coding from a team that is entirely out of touch with reality. This is supposed to be a classic BioWare RPG, but the developers completely forgot their own genre's roots. An RPG is about exploring, defeating enemies, and feeling like a powerful Sith Lord. Instead, they completely gutted open-world enemy XP to turn the main story into a tedious, unrewarding, slow crawl. The entire gameplay loop is intentionally rigged to force you into repetitive group queues or pressure you into buying pay-to-win cash shop boosts just to progress normally.
The story instances are incredibly poorly optimized. They turned basic class missions into a frustrating, artificial Dark Souls meat grinder due to broken scaling and bugged, invisible quest timers that auto-kill you if you don't beat a hidden clock. Your gear durability shatters instantly because the math is completely broken against higher-level quest mobs, and when you die, the garbage coding kicks you all the way back to a starting point a mile away. It actively punishes solo introverts who just want to sit back and enjoy the narrative in peace. Total waste of subscription money. Save your time and your cash—the people running this game are completely brain-dead.

SWTOR is probably one of the best MMO RPGs I've played in awhile! Classic gameplay from years ago when companies actually cared about the games they were making. Combat is relatively close to WoW and ESO Online. Cutscenes are actually good and I haven't skipped a single one because the story for your character is very interesting. UI is a little hard to understand at first, but after an hour or two, I caught on pretty quickly. The game is great and you can have a lot of fun just doing the Free-to-Play version!!!

Do I recommend this game? No. Unless you are like me, and your life has been insanely challenging over the last year to the point where your nervous system can literally only digest the equivalent of narrative saltine crackers. 

Thats what this game is. Bits of salt (that childhood promise and dream of being a smuggler or a bounty hunter or a 'not-dark-side' Sith), sprinkled across white crunchy soulless flour (endless hallways, combat that is about as engaging as a rat pushing a button that releases dopamine in his brain but asks nothing of you, and recycled npcs and enviorments over and over and over again) 

Saltines are great if you are unwell. Your tummy hurts. You fhrew up, and you need to get something, any kind of electrolites and easy to digest content into your body because your somatic body has been doing the equivalent of training for the olympics, then did a 7 month marathon in the real world, then crashed, then trained again, then did another 4 month marathon, then crashed again, and needs just the softest of the softest content in your wittle tummy. 

That is the only space in which i recommend this game. If you are either unwell, or insane.

Am I going to keep playing it after I post this review? Unfortunately yes. I am one of the aforementioned things, which one I am is up to perspective.

Truthfully though, it is helping my nervous system rest, my mind turn off, and me reconnect to a childhood dream i had. 

And I groan or laugh at almost every second of it, with the occasional, "okay i kind of liked that moment." 

I like this game because I don't like it. I have zero investment in whats happening. The stakes are beyond low. Its fun to make fun of it and occasionally be a little surprised and a little invested, rather than trying to get invested in a game i actually care about.

This is not KOTOR 3 but it's a damn good game. To not turn this review into a Star Wars ramble i'll try to keep it brief.

SWTOR is the singleplayer MMO of all time, a bioware experience with a side of MMO in the Star Wars universe that gives all that a true fan of this Sci-Fi IP could ask for, from living your own in universe fantasy to having an apartment on your favorite planet and truly customizing a character set into Star Wars tropes.

The economy is a bit predatory and the engine is definitely outdated but if you're willing to dump one month of subscription to unlock all the extra content and you're fine with accepting you're not going to be the best player in the galaxy, enjoying this game a story driven RPG can give you some of the best Star Wars writing you've ever seen.

Class questlines are not all built the same as some are definitely better than others but whatever you choose to engage with will resonate with you as long as you truly like and are interested in what you choose.

As for gameplay it's not something I can really add much in writing as it's your traditional MMO WoW'esque tab targeting combat. Not for everyone but also not bad, I personally really like it.

One of the other aspects worth mentioning is that it's probably one of the most welcoming communities, people are always eager to help new players and show them around.

This game is the best non-WoW MMORPG available today, and it's not even close.

No other MMO can say it has fully voiced cutscenes with Mass-Effect style dialogue trees that actually make a difference (even if isolated to the quest with no overarching consequences) in the end of each mission. The subscription is so user-friendly it's insane, with permanent access to every expansion released during, and prior to the purchase of a sub, with certain subscriber perks being kept after it ends because it marks you as a "Preferred" player. The devs put heart, soul, and love into the game, and its community. Is the economy pretty bad? Yeah, and the majority of crazy cool stuff is on the shop, but you can easily make a good looking character using the GTN (player-run flea market essentially). The community is still running somewhat strong with most areas (especially early-game) having an active chat with conversations going round-the-clock, even if some of the chats are a little... quirky. The combat, movement, skills/abilities, and art direction are all standard but enjoyable MMO design. With friends it's even more fun, although the lack of coop-able DLC missions is a MASSIVE missed opportunity.

Just for the class stories it's worth a play, and in my opinion worth a one-time sub. Give it a shot!

Star Wars: The Old Republic — It's All About the Story

If there is one thing you need to understand about Star Wars: The Old Republic, it's this:

This game is all about the story.

Whether you want to be good, evil, or somewhere in between is completely up to you. You can even change your mind during the game. Want to start as a good guy and slowly become the bad guy? You can. Want to play somewhere in the middle? You can do that too.

Or maybe you don't care about all that and just want to shoot things, fight enemies and have fun. That's fine too.

But honestly, the story is where this game shines.

It's fully voice-acted, with cinematic cutscenes and conversations that actually feel meaningful. You're not just clicking through walls of text to get your next random MMO quest. Your choices matter to the experience, and you build your own character, your own companions and, in a way, your own story.

Yes, technically you're one of thousands of players doing the same game. But it doesn't really feel that way.

And that's what makes SWTOR special.

There are plenty of random side quests, of course, because this is still an MMO. But you don't have to chase every single one. You can simply follow your class story, follow the main story and see where your adventure takes you.

Forget the usual MMO mentality for a moment.

Don't worry about completing every quest, getting the perfect gear or following some guide telling you exactly what to do.

Just play your character.

The game is definitely showing its age now. It was released a long time ago, and you can see that in some of the visuals and mechanics. But honestly, it can still look surprisingly beautiful in the right places.

And the sound design? Still fantastic, in my opinion. The music, weapons, environments and Star Wars atmosphere do a great job of making the universe feel alive.

Then there is the monetization.

There are things you can unlock through the Cartel Market, but there is also a lot you can unlock simply by playing the game. You don't necessarily have to spend money on everything.

And yes, you can even romance some of the characters if that's something you want to do. Personally, it's not really my thing, but the option is there.

Now for the question some people will probably ask:

"Is SWTOR woke?"

Honestly, I wouldn't say so.

There are strong female characters, but remember that this game has been around for a very long time. Strong women didn't suddenly appear because of some modern trend. They were already part of Star Wars long before the current discussion around "woke" games.

There are certainly some modern elements and themes that some people may interpret that way, but you don't have to focus on them. They aren't what the game is about, and for the most part they don't stop you from simply playing your character and enjoying the story.

So give it a try.

Don't approach SWTOR as just another MMO.

Approach it as a Star Wars RPG with MMO elements.

Pick your character. Pick your morality. Build your team. Follow your story.

And then just go do your thing.

That's where SWTOR is at its best.

STAR WARS: The Old Republic is a free-to-play MMORPG set in the Star Wars universe, and its biggest appeal for me is how much emphasis it puts on story. I can choose from different classes and experience separate campaigns built around characters, factions and the conflict between the Galactic Republic and Sith Empire. It feels much closer to playing through a series of Star Wars adventures than simply grinding through a typical MMO.

The class stories are easily the strongest part. Each class has its own narrative, companions and progression, which gives me a reason to care about the character I am playing. The dialogue choices also let me shape conversations and occasionally influence how situations develop, making the experience feel more personal than a standard quest-driven MMO.

The combat is fairly accessible and follows the familiar MMO formula of abilities, cooldowns and different roles. I can build my character around damage, healing or tanking depending on the class, and learning how to use my abilities efficiently becomes more important as I reach harder content. It is not the fastest combat system around, but it works well alongside the story.

The companion system is another feature I really enjoy. I can recruit different characters during my adventures, build relationships with them and bring them along to help in combat. Their personalities and conversations add extra life to the journey, and I like that companions can feel like actual characters rather than simple NPCs following me around.

The multiplayer content gives the game plenty of additional activities. Flashpoints, operations and PvP provide ways to play with other people after I have spent time progressing through the story. Working with a group to complete a difficult encounter can be rewarding, although the experience naturally depends on finding players who communicate and cooperate.

The biggest weakness is the age and complexity of the game. STAR WARS: The Old Republic has been running for many years, so there are a huge number of systems, currencies, missions and pieces of content to understand. The interface and some aspects of the presentation also feel dated compared with newer MMORPGs, even though the Star Wars setting still gives it plenty of personality.

The free-to-play structure can also be restrictive. I can experience a substantial amount of the game without paying, but some features, content and conveniences are tied to subscriptions or purchases. Players who want the complete MMO experience may therefore end up spending money beyond the initial free download.

Overall, STAR WARS: The Old Republic remains one of the strongest story-focused MMORPGs I have played. I love the class stories, companions, dialogue choices and huge amount of Star Wars content, while the aging presentation, complicated systems and free-to-play restrictions can make getting started more difficult. For anyone who enjoys Star Wars and wants an RPG with a genuinely substantial story, though, there is an enormous amount to enjoy.
